## 1. shen2026aiformaterials pages 1-4 (Context ID: pqac-00000031)

13 August 2026
AI for Materials Science at Industrial Scale

Kevin Shen, Xiaopei Qin, Jonathan Scharf, Yunya Zhang, Chun Li, Qichao Hu, Kang Xu, Yumin Zhang


Abstract

Materials science has hit an inﬂection point with AI, drawing an intense ﬂurry of interest and
enormous scales of capital across academia, tech, and traditional industry. To look forward
we ﬁrst take a tour through the development of modern technologies powering this new
age, from shared databases to foundation machine learned interaction potentials to agentic
laboratories. We conceptualize the technology stack as 3 tiers (data foundations, tools, and
orchestration), trace their rapid maturation into infrastructure, and map the modern industrial
ecosystem and how prominent parties are making diﬀerent bets. We use our battery research
programme to illustrate how these AI tools can come together in an industrial setting, and
point out emerging areas stemming from challenges in materials development and translation.
Speciﬁcally, we observe that AI progress has to date concentrated on candidate generation
and low latency measurements that may or may not correlate with longer time horizon
materials development. Drawing on lessons from pharmaceuticals, specialty chemicals design,
and semiconductor design automation, we argue that the potential of AI will only be materialized
with key contributions from materials scientists: richer mechanistic characterization and
judicious encoding of downstream constraints.

https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv.15007406/v1         AI for Materials Science at Industrial Scale

     Kevin Shen   1, Xiaopei Qin1, Jonathan Scharf   , Yunya Zhang   , Chun Li,
                    Qichao Hu, Kang Xu   , Yumin Zhang∗

               SES AI Corporation, 35 Cabot Road, Woburn, MA 01810, USA

                                 1These authors contributed equally.

                               ∗Corresponding author: yumin.zhang@ses.ai

                              August 11, 2026



Abstract

Materials science has hit an inflection point with AI, drawing an intense flurry of interest and

enormous scales of capital across academia, tech, and traditional industry. To look forward we

first take a tour through the development of modern technologies powering this new age, from

shared databases to foundation machine learned interaction potentials to agentic laboratories. We

conceptualize the technology stack as 3 tiers (data foundations, tools, and orchestration), trace

their rapid maturation into infrastructure, and map the modern industrial ecosystem and how

prominent parties are making different bets. We use our battery research programme to illustrate
how these AI tools can come together in an industrial setting, and point out emerging areas

stemming from challenges in materials development and translation. Specifically, we observe that
AI progress has to date concentrated on candidate generation and low latency measurements
that may or may not correlate with longer time horizon materials development. Drawing on

lessons from pharmaceuticals, specialty chemicals design, and semiconductor design automation,

we argue that the potential of AI will only be materialized with key contributions from materials

scientists: richer mechanistic characterization and judicious encoding of downstream constraints.


1  Introduction: Why Now

Fifteen years after the Materials Genome Initiative promised to halve the time from discovery
to deployment [1], the bet is back—larger, louder, and wrapped in a different name. Machine

learning for materials is not new [2]; what changed is that search, simulation, and orchestration
became shared infrastructure rather than bespoke methods.  In one week in July 2026 the
U.S. government announced a coordinated architecture for AI-driven science: the Genesis

Mission’s federal commitments across more than fifteen agencies, DOE’s first project selections,
and the National Science Foundation’s award of twenty Programmable Cloud Laboratory
nodes—an estimated $379 million over four years, with awards starting August 1 [3, 4, 5, 6].
The lineage is explicit. The Genesis programme’s materials challenge, “Designing Materials

with Predictable Functionality,” asks for “materials design that iteratively couple[s] prediction,


                                         1synthesis, characterization, and analysis” and claims that tight integration “could significantly
reduce time to market in manufacturing—from many years to decades down to months to a
few years,” including batteries [7]. The White House’s Science: A New Golden Age report,

published the day before, puts the doctrine in one sentence: government’s job is to “shape the

arena rather than direct discovery,” because “the private sector possesses capabilities

public institutions must learn to leverage rather than replicate.” [6]

    Private capital heard the same music. Since September 2025, disclosed venture funding for

AI-for-materials companies totals, by our own tally, roughly $1.98–2.29 billion, with three firms
accounting for about 87% of it [8, 9].1 Andreessen Horowitz led Periodic Labs’ $300 million

founding round with a thesis any MRS reader can quote back: “The data in the literature is

fundamentally insufficient”—high noise in formation enthalpies, negative results unpublished,

epistemic uncertainty that “can’t be collapsed without running an experiment.” Their remedy:
“nature becomes the reinforcement learning environment.” The same memo names
industries worth “roughly $15 trillion of global GDP”—sectors AI has “barely touched

because you can’t transform them with models trained only on text.” [8] Charles Yang, writing on

Substack, put the public-private comparison in plain terms: venture investment into autonomous

labs for materials and chemistry in a single year is “comparable to the annual NSF budget

for materials, chemistry, and physics”—with the caveat, which he states himself, that VC

rounds deploy over years while agency budgets are annual. [9]
  We are not skeptical of the ambition. Energy transition, human health, semiconductor
sovereignty, defence materials—every serious roadmap for the next decade runs through a

materials bottleneck someone has to break. The historical record is full of proof that concentrated

effort pays off: lithium-ion cells from Sony’s commercial launch in 1991 to today’s gigafactories;

high-k gate dielectrics that let CMOS scale at 45 nm and beyond; carbon fibre from aerospace
curiosity to wind-turbine structural default; photoresist chemistry that tracks every node the

lithography industry prints. Those wins go beyond paper novelty. They were configurations—a

compound in a process, on a line, in a device—that survived qualification and then scaled.

a Cloud-Hosted Commercial Robot Driven by

Matteo Manica1, Alain C. Vaucher 1,2, Carlo Baldassari1,2, Antonio Cardinale1, Aleksandros Sobczyk1, Alessandro

Abstract

The concept of self-driving chemical laboratories builds on top of two technologies: robust artiﬁcial
intelligence models that translate synthesis designs into executable instructions, potentially
incorporating instrument feedback, and robotic workstations capable of executing those procedures
seamlessly and without human intervention. Here we present RoboRXN, a cloud-native framework
that uniﬁes transformer-based retrosynthesis and chemical action extraction or prediction models
with a commercially available synthesis robot and in-line high-resolution LC–MS. Across more than
3000 actions autonomously executed, we analyzed in details 33 reactions distributed among 10
single-step reactions and 9 multi-step campaigns. Eightythree percent of single-steps and all two-step
routes succeeded without parameter adjustment; a branched four-step synthesis completed after
one on-deck modiﬁcation. Regardless of the overall success, we systematically encountered three
recurring bottlenecks: hardware rigidity, execution-level data gaps, and slow physical feedback,
which are seldom reported in the literature, despite being common to many commercial platform
design. We delineate how each failure surfaced, quantify its impact on yield or throughput, and
outline engineering and data-centric remedies. By publishing both the successes and the blind spots,
we hope to redirect community eﬀort from one-oﬀ demonstrations toward robust, transparent, and
widely adoptable AI-driven laboratories.

                                       3Introduction


Combining artificial intelligence (AI) and laboratory automation is often presented as a fric-

tionless path toward an era of self-driving discovery, an appealing narrative in a field fighting

with escalating costs, an acute reproducibility crisis!1,2 and unprecedented societal demand

for rapid molecular innovation.3 Among the technologies developed in recent years,4–11 lan-

guage models, especially those trained on domain-specific corpora,12–15 and increasingly their

general-purpose counterparts,16–18 have emerged as state-of-the-art tools for designing syn-

thetic routes entirely in silico. At the same time, robotic platforms execute synthetic routes

remotely, seemingly parallelizing months of bench work.19–22 Yet the dominant narrative

around these successes is strikingly one-sided: milestone demonstrations are celebrated, but

the routine frictions, dead-ends and design mismatches that still derail autonomy at scale

are rarely discussed. In this work, we embrace the “full-stack” view, celebrating what works

while candidly reporting the challenges that stall adoption, believing a transparent account-

ing of failures is itself a catalyst for innovation.


Over the past five years, a growing body of research has shown that AI models can instruct

and, in some cases, even guide robotic chemists, marking a clear convergence of artificial intel-

ligence and automation.21,23–31 Representative self-driving laboratories (SDL) span multiple

domains, from closed-loop materials discovery platforms to accelerated discovery autonomous

platforms,25,32,33 highlighting the breadth of approaches and the importance of robust au-

tomation and provenance. For a broader overview of SDLs, we refer the reader to recent

reviews34,35 and the references therein. In contrast, our goal in the present work is to focus

specifically on cloud-mediated execution and the integration layer between transformer-based

planning models for chemical synthesis and a commercial automation workstation, and to

report the execution-level constraints and failure modes that emerge under realistic broad-

range operation. While many of the operational lessons discussed in this paper apply broadly

## 1. shen2026aiformaterials pages 14-17 (Context ID: pqac-00000046)

y 100× and 800× at batch in NVIDIA’s own benchmarks [122]. ENEOS reports screening

some 10 million liquid-immersion candidates and 100 million oxygen-evolution candidates within
weeks, and Universal Display puts conformer search up to 10,000× over conventional methods
[123]. Here, open-source software is NVIDIA’s distribution strategy: keep scientific work on

NVIDIA silicon, and the next wave of AI-for-science tools gets built there too.

   Raise the ceiling and let the domains follow. Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic
are running a third bet. Their wager is that the scarce resource is not any materials-specific

asset but general scientific reasoning—so the investment goes into pushing what a frontier model


                                        13can imagine and prove at all, on the expectation that domains inherit the gains. Their evidence

is tantalizing, though it ranges well beyond materials science. DeepMind’s GNoME enlarged the

stable-crystal map [60], and its 2026 output ran to a one-megabase-context sequence-to-function

genome model [124], a multi-agent Co-Scientist that proposed drug candidates for acute myeloid

leukaemia and new targets for liver fibrosis [125], and a Deep Think agent that autonomously

settled four open problems from the Erdős database and produced a paper on eigenweights in

arithmetic geometry [126]. OpenAI’s August 2026 Astra announcement reported ten resolutions

or substantial advances on long-standing open problems across fields including high-dimensional
geometry, coding theory, group theory, operator algebras, quantum complexity, and lattice
cryptography—each argument formalized in a Lean certificate, at a total token cost for all
ten that the company put near $2,000 [127].  Anthropic’s Claude Science, in beta since
30 June 2026, bundles provenance, HPC job submission, and curated skills for genomics,

single-cell analysis, proteomics, structural biology, and cheminformatics [128]; its own

chemistry research reports Claude models matching or beating ChemDraw and MestReNova at

NMR prediction, hitting sub-peak spacings within half a hertz roughly 80% of the time against

26–35% for those incumbents [129].
   Take that evidence seriously and its shape is still instructive. A Lean certificate checks in

seconds; an NMR peak list is a file. Every one of these results comes from a domain where the
verifier is cheap—where a claim can be graded without a physical lab. Materials is precisely

where that property fails: no one can formally verify that a cathode survives a thousand cycles

without running the experiment. So the fields that inherited these gains first are the ones whose

ground truth is symbolic or already digitized, and the frontier labs’ materials-adjacent output

tracks that constraint closely. OpenAI’s public chemistry result is the June 2026 collaboration

with Molecule.one on a primary sulfonamide Chan–Lam coupling: 10,080 microscale reactions

raised mean yield from 16.6% to 25.2%, with the gain confirmed in eleven of fourteen bench-scale

reproductions [130]—reversible optimization on a known reaction class, not a new material headed
for qualification. Anthropic’s cheminformatics is small-molecule work rather than inorganic-

crystal or process-qualification tooling; materials access exists only if a user wires it: the Materials

Project now ships an MCP server with its API client [13, 131], but nothing is pre-packaged the

way genomics is. Google’s July 2026 Genesis portfolio contribution lists AlphaFold and genomics

tools and no materials foundation model [132], and its December 2025 UK memorandum for an

automated superconductor laboratory remains voluntary and non-binding, without a named site

as of mid-2026 [133].

  What none of them sell. Everything on offer here is computation. Azure rents queue time,

UMA and ALCHEMI ship as downloads, and a frontier model’s answer can be regenerated for

the price of the tokens. Even the giveaways charge eventually: Meta bought a seat at CuspAI’s
closed data, and NVIDIA collects because weights still need silicon. But the money changes

hands for corpora and compute—no one sells the proprietary data, the qualification testing, or

the process of record. Not one launch surveyed above names a material that cleared qualification.





                                        143.2  The Industrial Bets

If Microsoft Discovery and Claude Science can rent simulation, orchestration, and cheminformatics
for a subscription fee, why did venture capital put roughly $1.98–2.29 billion into AI-for-
materials companies between September 2025 and July 2026—with three firms taking about

87% of it (§1)? Investors did not miss middle-layer commoditization. They are placing conflicting

bets on which segment of the industrial path is still rate-limiting, and therefore on what

kind of win is worth optimizing for.
   Each actor is a resource-allocation thesis centered on a different scarce asset. Ordered by

what they claim is missing, the bets escalate—from data that does not exist yet, through data

that exists but is locked up, to a product a customer has already paid for—while two positions
sit outside that axis: the tool sellers who arm every bet, and the public floor beneath every

private thesis.
  The data does not exist yet: manufacture it. Periodic Labs pairs frontier models
with autonomous laboratories [134] because, in Andreessen Horowitz’s September 2025 seed
thesis, literature formation enthalpies are too noisy, negative results vanish, and epistemic
uncertainty that matters cannot be collapsed without running an experiment [8]. The remedy
quoted in §1—nature as the reinforcement-learning environment—is a bet that proprietary

loops, not rented simulation, are the moat. Periodic co-founder Ekin Doğuş Çubuk, who co-led

GNoME [60], names a narrower bottleneck: robotic powder handling is “quite commoditized,”

while automated characterization is not [135]. Lila Sciences scales the same thesis through
instruments under AI control [136], with its flagship Cambridge AI Science Factory slated to
open in 2026 [137] and three DOE Genesis Phase I awards in July 2026 [138]. Radical AI,
co-founded by A-Lab PI Gerbrand Ceder, is the throughput variant: closed-loop inorganic

synthesis as industrial infrastructure [139].

  The data exists but is enclosed: license and federate it. CuspAI shares Periodic’s
diagnosis and differs on acquisition.  Its July 2026 AI Materials Foundry federates 31

industrial founding partners, a 14-member laboratory network, and three structural-data

providers—CCDC, FIZ Karlsruhe’s ICSD, and Wiley—in a consortium of more than forty-five
partners overall, while keeping partner programmes in walled instances [121]. Periodic would

generate negative results in-house; CuspAI compounds Foundry outcomes onto licensed archives
and open models such as Meta’s UMA [39].  Meta’s dual role—open-weight vendor above,

founding partner inside a closed-data consortium here—is the rent-versus-enclose tension in one
logo. What remains open is whether a confidentiality-guaranteed federation can compound a

shared model or become parallel consulting with a common interface.

  The scarce thing is integration itself. XtalPi runs its own robotic laboratories under AI

control [140]—an executable synthesis record at scale. DP Technology and its AI-for-Science
Institute play the same integration game from China: large atomic models, Bohrium cloud,

and Uni-Lab OS spanning simulation through agent orchestration [141]. Deep Principle and
Kaiwuji anchor the Asia cohort with the same full-pipeline ambition as Periodic and Radical

[142, 143].

  The scarce asset is already held. BASF and Merck KGaA hold decades of plant and
formulation records and the hard problem of qualifying a material for production [144, 145].


                                        15Both have leaned into the experiment-planning tradition—BASF co-develops the open-source
Bayesian-optimization library BoFire, and Merck released BayBE—because the durable asset
is process data, not a foundation model [146, 147]. Merck’s AIDDISON generative platform

and SYNTHIA retrosynthesis engine sit atop the same proprietary substrate [148, 87]. Toyota
Research Institute’s Accelerated Materials Design and Discovery programme spent roughly

$70 million across seventeen university projects from 2017 to 2025, funding at least forty-five
PhD theses whose alumni now include some twenty professors and the leaders of materials
startups [149]. TRI’s retrospectives are candid on materials output: they have led a polymer
campaign with “no winning polymer,” [150] and the best candidate found in a search for a
disordered-rocksalt cathode “decays too quickly for the material to be commercially viable.”

[151]

   Nothing here is scarce enough to own. The horizontal suppliers make the inverse bet:

sell tools to everyone and let the customers fight over the scarce assets. SandboxAQ sells La

                Materials discovery lays the foundation for many technological advancements. The prediction and

                nity, as follows. (i) Automated Rietveld analysis of powder x-ray diﬀraction data is not yet reliable. Future

                ting, would be very helpful, not only for autonomous materials discovery but also for the community in
              general. (ii) We ﬁnd that disorder in materials is often neglected in predictions. The predicted compounds
              investigated herein have all their elemental components located on distinct crystallographic positions but
               in reality, elements can share crystallographic sites, resulting in higher-symmetry space groups and—very
           often—known alloys or solid solutions. This error might be related to the diﬃculty of modeling disorder
               in a computationally economical way and needs to be addressed both by computational and experimen-
                 tal material scientists. We ﬁnd that two thirds of the claimed successful materials in Szymanski et al. are
               likely to be known compositionally disordered versions of the predicted ordered compounds. We highlight
             important issues in materials discovery, computational chemistry, and autonomous interpretation of x-ray
              diﬀraction. We discuss concepts of materials discovery from an experimentalist point of view, which we
            hope will be helpful for the community to further advance this important new aspect of our ﬁeld.

Leeman et al. (2024), a peer-reviewed PRX Energy perspective, describe the original A-Lab paper as classifying 36 compounds as “successes” and seven as “partial successes,” totaling 43 claimed outcomes, and as implying a 78% success rate. Their critique disputes that interpretation: they report significant problems with 42 of the 43 cases, identifying CaFe2(PO4)2O as the sole exception in their assessment. They state that only three materials—MnAgO2, Y3In2Ga3O12, and CaFe2(PO4)2O—could reasonably be considered successfully synthesized as predicted, although all had been reported previously. Under their broader accounting, they give a 3/58 (5%) success rate; under a strict definition requiring genuinely unpublished materials, they say none would count as discoveries. The excerpt also reports that, after Leeman et al. raised concerns, the Ceder group conceded that A-Lab did not meet “human standards,” while continuing to defend it as a rapid preliminary proof-of-makeability system. This passage does not itself provide a detailed formal correction or complete reply from the A-Lab authors, nor does it explicitly establish a separate “40 accepted and 4 inconclusive” accounting; those figures should therefore be checked against the original A-Lab paper and its subsequent peer-reviewed response. The numerical claims here are Leeman et al.’s critique and should be labeled as disputed rather than treated as settled fact.

PRX Energy, Mar 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1103/prxenergy.3.011002, doi:10.1103/prxenergy.3.011002. This article has 219 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes the original A-Lab claim in Szymanski et al.: A-Lab reportedly synthesized 41 of 58 predicted targets autonomously within 17 days, a 71% success rate; with human intervention, this rose to 43 successful syntheses, or 78%. The work was presented as the autonomous discovery of 43 novel materials. Leeman et al. (PRX Energy 3, 011002, 2024), however, dispute that interpretation. Their perspective states that their analysis of all 43 products found four recurring problems and concluded that none could be established as genuinely new materials. They emphasize two principal issues: automated Rietveld analysis of powder X-ray diffraction was not yet reliable, and computational predictions often neglected chemical disorder. In particular, predicted ordered structures may correspond experimentally to higher-symmetry, compositionally disordered known alloys or solid solutions; Leeman et al. judged that approximately two-thirds of the claimed successes were likely such known disordered materials. This excerpt does not contain the subsequent correction, author reply, or the later classification using the figures 36, 40, and 4 inconclusive. Those points therefore require separate peer-reviewed sourcing and should be presented as a disagreement or evolving reassessment, rather than treating Leeman et al.’s critique as definitively settled.

This excerpt documents Leeman et al.’s peer-reviewed critique of the A-Lab high-throughput synthesis paper, but it does not provide the original A-Lab paper’s complete discovery claim, any subsequent A-Lab reply or correction, or figures specifically labeled “36, 40, 4 inconclusive.” The review states that it examined 43 reported materials, including partial successes. It identifies recurring problems: for 24 of 36 compounds in the relevant analysis, the synthesized material may have had a known disordered structure rather than the predicted cation-ordered structure; three of 36 were allegedly compounds already reported in the ICSD; and some claimed structures were inconsistent with powder-diffraction intensities or the supplied CIF files. For Mg3NiO4, the authors argue that the product was probably a disordered MgO–NiO solid solution, not ordered Mg3NiO4, while acknowledging that the ordered phase might still be synthesizable. For Mg3MnNi3O8, they report poor agreement with the proposed ordered model and possible multiphase material. For layered KMn3O6, they say the supplied structure differs from the prediction and that the presence of ordered K or buckled layers remains unclear. These are criticisms and interpretations by Leeman et al., not settled facts; comparison with the original A-Lab publication and any published response is required to present the disagreement fairly.

This excerpt documents Leeman et al.’s critique of the A-Lab dataset, but it does not provide the original A-Lab “43 materials” claim, any subsequent A-Lab correction or reply, or the later accounting involving 40 materials and 4 inconclusive cases. In the material shown, Leeman et al. state that the A-Lab paper discussed 58 compounds: 15 failures, 7 partial successes (less than 50 wt% in the final product), and 36 claimed successes, including two successful only after human intervention. They report that 35 of those 36 claimed successes suffered from at least one identified analytical problem. The listed problems include very poor Rietveld fits that cannot establish structure or purity, changing the predicted structure to match observed diffraction, and claiming ordered cation structures without evidence for ordering when known disordered compounds exist. The authors also argue that treating samples above 50% purity as successful is anomalous relative to normal solid-state chemistry practice. This excerpt provides the basis of Leeman et al.’s peer-reviewed critique of the A-Lab’s claimed discoveries, but it does not state the original numerical claim of 43 materials or report a subsequent A-Lab correction/reply distinguishing 36, 40, and 4 inconclusive cases. Leeman et al. explain that A-Lab appears to define novelty as a Materials Project entry marked “theoretical” and absent from the ICSD, a criterion they regard as open to criticism because the databases have important coverage limitations. They argue that predicted structures may simply represent ordered variants of known disordered compounds, so cation ordering must be experimentally demonstrated. More broadly, they contend that discovery claims require falsification tests against plausible known phases, unreacted starting materials, contaminants, and competing compositions—not merely confirmatory evidence. Powder XRD may be unable to distinguish candidate structures, and even a good Rietveld fit does not establish that the modeled structure is correct. Thus, the excerpt supports reporting the critique as a peer-reviewed challenge to the original claims, while labeling any later A-Lab correction or reply—and the specific 36/40/4 classification—as a separate development requiring its own source rather than treating Leeman et al.’s critique as settled fact.

Abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Autonomous laboratories increasingly enable materials synthesis at scale, but traditional high‐throughput characterization workflows remain limited by the need for expert chemical intuition to distinguish plausible interpretations from formally good but chemically incorrect fits. We present an automated interpretation framework that combines probabilistic inference with automated chemical reasoning for phase identification from powder x‐ray diffraction (PXRD). The framework evaluates multiple candidate interpretations using diffraction pattern‐based metrics. It then refines these likelihoods using chemically‐informed priors derived from composition balance and a large language model (LLM)–based plausibility estimate with human‐readable justification and also produces a trustworthiness score. In a blinded multi‐project benchmark, the framework's top‐ranked interpretation was selected over the lowest‐ baseline in 93% of cases where evaluators expressed a clear preference (95% CI: [78%, 98%], ). Trust decisions made by the framework aligned with expert judgment in approximately 75%–80% of cases. In a second evaluation, the framework systematically identified cases where lowest‐ interpretations were chemically implausible and surfaced credible alternatives to historically ambiguous samples. By reframing phase identification as a problem of probabilistic reasoning and trust‐aware decision making, this work demonstrates how chemical intuition can be automated and scaled.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>Materials science is at the crossroad between fundamental and applied sciences. Whether enabling clean energy, next-generation computing, or advanced manufacturing, it shapes the tools we use and the systems we build. As our societies undergo rapid digital, environmental, and technological transitions, materials science becomes even more central. It's a space where innovation can respond to practical challenges while aligning with broader social values. In the European context, that means supporting sustainability, openness, and solidarity -while also strengthening competitiveness.This roadmap explores how digital tools-especially simulation, data science, and AI-are transforming materials research, in connection with the twin digital and energy transition. The digital transition refers to the widespread adoption of digital technologies and data-driven methods across sectors, while the green (or energy) transition focuses on shifting toward sustainable, lowcarbon energy systems-together forming what is often called the twin transition, a joint effort to make economies both smarter and more sustainable.The Roadmap outlines both the technical directions and the cultural shifts needed to make this transformation inclusive and effective. Chapters span from atomic-scale simulations to advanced experimentation, from reproducibility to intelligent optimization, and from institutional reform to education for the next generation.Importantly, this isn't a single viewpoint. The document brings together a wide range of voices: researchers from different disciplines, working across length and time scales. It includes early-career scientists and senior experts. Enabled by activities supported by European Cooperation in Science and Technology (COST), it reflects a commitment to gender and geographic diversity. This plurality doesn't just enrich the content-it makes the vision more robust and relevant.We hope this collection serves not just as a guide, but as an invitation to collaborate-across fields, sectors, and borders-as we reimagine the future of materials science in a digital age.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Formulation development still consumes a disproportionate share of the time and material spent on a drug candidate, largely because the relationships linking molecular structure, excipient choice, composition and process to product performance are nonlinear and only partly understood. Machine learning (ML) has entered this space along three fronts: numerical representation of molecules and formulations, prediction of developability properties such as solubility and amorphous stability, and, most recently, closed-loop experimentation in which a model chooses the next experiment and a robotic platform performs it. This review traces that progression using only in silico, physicochemical and in vitro evidence, and deliberately excludes studies whose conclusions rest on human or animal data. Across the literature, predictive accuracy for well-posed physicochemical tasks now approaches experimental reproducibility, and dosage-form models trained on a few hundred to several thousand curated records reach useful accuracy for solid dispersions, cyclodextrin complexes, long-acting injectables, printed dosage forms and spectroscopic dissolution testing. The dominant constraint, however, is no longer the algorithm. Formulation data are scarce, heterogeneous, mined from publications that rarely report failure, and routinely evaluated with splits that overstate generalisation. Bayesian optimisation and self-driving laboratories matter chiefly because they change how data are produced: reported campaigns reached target formulations after sampling a few per cent of a design space, or with less than half the experiments of conventional design of experiments. The review argues that the next advance depends on system-level representations of the formulation, standardised and FAIR data including negative results, honest uncertainty estimates, and validation practices aligned with the credibility frameworks now emerging from regulators.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Clinical robustness is critical to the safe deployment of medical Large Language Models (LLMs), but key questions remain about how LLMs and humans may differ in response to the real-world variability typified by clinical settings. To address this, we introduce MedPerturb, a dataset designed to systematically evaluate medical LLMs under controlled perturbations of clinical input. MedPerturb consists of clinical vignettes spanning a range of pathologies, each transformed along three axes: (1) gender modifications (e.g., gender-swapping or gender-removal); (2) style variation (e.g., uncertain phrasing or colloquial tone); and (3) format changes (e.g., LLM-generated multi-turn conversations or summaries). With MedPerturb, we release a dataset of 800 clinical contexts grounded in realistic input variability, outputs from four LLMs, and three human expert reads per clinical context. We use MedPerturb in two case studies to reveal how shifts in gender identity cues, language style, or format reflect diverging treatment selections between humans and LLMs. We find that LLMs are more sensitive to gender and style perturbations while human annotators are more sensitive to LLM-generated format perturbations such as clinical summaries. Our results highlight the need for evaluation frameworks that go beyond static benchmarks to assess the similarity between human clinician and LLM decisions under the variability characteristic of clinical settings.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    To close the gap between the rates of computational screening and experimental realization of novel materials
                    <jats:sup>1,2</jats:sup>
                    , we introduce the A-Lab, an autonomous laboratory for the solid-state synthesis of inorganic powders. This platform uses computations, historical data from the literature, machine learning (ML) and active learning to plan and interpret the outcomes of experiments performed using robotics. Over 17 days of continuous operation, the A-Lab realized 36 compounds from a set of 57 targets including a variety of oxides and phosphates that were identified using large-scale ab initio phase-stability data from the Materials Project and Google DeepMind. Synthesis recipes were proposed by natural-language models trained on the literature and optimized using an active-learning approach grounded in thermodynamics. Analysis of the failed syntheses provides direct and actionable suggestions to improve current techniques for materials screening and synthesis design. The high success rate demonstrates the effectiveness of artificial-intelligence-driven platforms for autonomous materials synthesis and motivates further integration of computations, historical knowledge and robotics.
                  </jats:p>

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

Abstract:
The introduction of the capability to “program” a biological system is referred to as Engineered biology and can be compared to the introduction of the internet and the capability of programming a computer. Engineered biology is supported by a digital infrastructure that includes data, data storage, computer-dependent laboratory equipment, internet-connected communication networks, and supply chains. This connectivity is important. It can improve workflows and enhance productivity. At the same time and unlike computer programs, biological systems introduce unique threats as they can self-assemble, self-repair, and self-replicate. The aim of this paper is to systematically review the cyber implications of engineered biology. This includes cyber-bio opportunities and threats as engineered biology continues to integrate into cyberspace. We used a systematic search methodology to review the academic literature, and supplemented this with a review of opensource materials and “grey” literature that is not disseminated by academic publishers. A comprehensive search of articles published in or after 2017 until the 21st of October 2022 found 52 studies that focus on implications of engineered biology to cyberspace. The search was conducted using search engines that index over 60 databases–databases that specifically cover the information security, and biology literatures, as well as the wider set of academic disciplines. Across these 52 articles, we identified a total of 7 cyber opportunities including automated bio-foundries and 4 cyber threats such as Artificial Intelligence misuse and biological dataset targeting. We highlight the 4 main types of cyberbiosecurity solutions identified in the literature and we suggest a total of 9 policy recommendations that can be utilized by various entities, including governments, to ensure that cyberbiosecurity remains frontline in a growing bioeconomy.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping scientific research by accelerating discovery and enabling the analysis of complex data that traditional methods struggle to handle. This review examines over 310,000 journal articles and patents from the CAS Content Collection (2015–2025), with a focus on, biomedical research, and materials science.  Our data-supported trend analysis finds that since 2020, AI-related publications have surged across both academic and industrial domains. Traditional machine learning (ML) methods, such as decision trees, random forests, and support vector machines, remain foundational, particularly in molecular property prediction and classification tasks. However, there is an increased adoption of advanced neural network architectures, including graph neural networks for molecular representation and generative models for de novo compound design. Hybrid and ensemble approaches that integrate traditional algorithms with deep learning are increasingly favored for their robustness and adaptability. Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT, BERT, and GEMINI are transforming literature mining, hypothesis generation, and experimental planning. Domain-specific models such as AlphaFold and chemical language models enable breakthroughs in protein structure prediction and reaction outcome forecasting.  Industrial chemistry and chemical engineering are increasingly contributing to AI-driven academic publications, while biochemistry patents have grown eightfold, reflecting AI’s dual impact on discovery and commercialization. Despite these advances, challenges remain, particularly in data privacy, quality, interpretability of black-box models, and uncertainty quantification. These findings highlight AI’s transition from descriptor-based approaches to end-to-end learning systems, offering essential insights for researchers and policymakers navigating its transformative role in science.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Materials science has hit an inflection point with AI, drawing an intense flurry of interest and enormous scales of capital across academia, tech, and traditional industry. To look forward we first take a tour through the development of modern technologies powering this new age, from shared databases to foundation machine learned interaction potentials to agentic laboratories. We conceptualize the technology stack as 3 tiers (data foundations, tools, and orchestration), trace their rapid maturation into infrastructure, and map the modern industrial ecosystem and how prominent parties are making different bets. We use our battery research programme to illustrate how these AI tools can come together in an industrial setting, and point out emerging areas stemming from challenges in materials development and translation. Specifically, we observe that AI progress has to date concentrated on candidate generation and low latency measurements that may or may not correlate with longer time horizon materials development. Drawing on lessons from pharmaceuticals, specialty chemicals design, and semiconductor design automation, we argue that the potential of AI will only be materialized with key contributions from materials scientists: richer mechanistic characterization and judicious encoding of downstream constraints.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the life sciences has accelerated significantly between 2022 and 2026, accompanied by global investment exceeding USD 100 billion and widespread expectations of a transformative impact in drug discovery. Despite these advances, the extent to which AI has improved clinical outcomes remains unclear. This study presents a structured narrative review evaluating the economic, technical, clinical, and regulatory dimensions of AI adoption in drug discovery. Current evidence indicates that clinical attrition rates remain high, with approximately 90% of drug candidates entering clinical development failing to achieve regulatory approval. Although AI systems such as AlphaFold have achieved high structural prediction accuracy, with predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT) scores exceeding 90 for well-structured proteins and root mean square deviation (RMSD) values comparable to experimental methods, limitations persist in modelling protein dynamics, post-translational modifications, and protein–ligand interactions. Clinical case studies demonstrate that while AI can accelerate early-stage discovery timelines, these advantages do not consistently translate into improved late-stage success rates. Furthermore, reproducibility challenges, limited data transparency, and regulatory gaps continue to constrain reliable implementation. These findings suggest that AI in drug discovery is currently in a transitional phase characterised by high investment but limited validated clinical impact. Future progress will depend on strengthening validation frameworks, improving data sharing practices, and aligning regulatory standards with real-world clinical performance.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming drug discovery and development by enhancing the speed and precision of identifying drug candidates and optimizing their efficacy. This review evaluates the application of AI in various stages of drug discovery, from hit identification to lead optimization, and its impact on clinical outcomes. The objective is to provide insights into the role of AI across therapeutic areas and assess its contributions to improving clinical trial efficiency and pharmaceutical outcomes. Methods: A systematic review followed PRISMA guidelines to analyze studies published between 2015 and 2025, focusing on AI in drug discovery and development. A comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases to identify studies employing AI techniques. The studies were categorized based on AI methods, clinical phase, and therapeutic area. The percentages of AI methods used, clinical phase stages, and the therapeutic regions were analyzed to identify trends. Results: AI methods included machine learning (ML) at 40.9%, molecular modeling and simulation (MMS) at 20.7%, and deep learning (DL) at 10.3%. Oncology accounted for the majority of studies (72.8%), followed by dermatology (5.8%) and neurology (5.2%). In clinical phases, 39.3% of studies were in the preclinical stage, 23.1% in Clinical Phase I, and 11.0% in the transitional phase. Clinical outcome reporting was observed in 45% of studies, with 97% reporting industry partnerships. Conclusions: AI significantly enhances drug discovery and development, improving drug efficacy and clinical trial outcomes. Future work should focus on expanding AI applications into underrepresented therapeutic areas and refining models to handle complex biological systems.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Background: Traditional animal models in preclinical pharmacology show limited predictive accuracy for human outcomes due to interspecies differences, contributing to high drug attrition rates and ethical concerns. Recent regulatory changes have pushed the development of alternative, human-centered methods.Objective: To comprehensively investigate and evaluate novel non-animal approaches for establishing pharmacological safety and efficacy, such as organ-on-a-chip technologies, in vitro systems, and in silico models.Methods: A narrative evaluation of existing literature was conducted, concentrating on the technological principles, pharmacological applications, predictive performance, and regulatory acceptance of alternative testing strategies.Results: Compared with traditional 2D cultures, advanced in vitro models such as 3D organoids and iPSC-derived cells exhibit greater physiological relevance. Rapid, economical, and high-throughput predictions are made possible by in silico methods such as QSAR, PBPK modeling, and AI-based technologies. With improved translational fidelity, organ-on-a-chip technologies mimic the dynamic microenvironments of human organs. Strong, mechanism-based safety assessment frameworks are produced by integrated testing procedures that combine these methods. But there are still issues with scalability, validation, and standards.Conclusion: With growing regulatory approval for their future application, the incorporation of alternative approaches signifies a paradigm change toward more ethical, human-centered, and predictive drug development.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>This chapter establishes the technological and definitional groundwork necessary for the legal analysis that follows. It traces the historical milestones in AI development and examines the evolving attempts to define AI, highlighting the absence of a unitary legal definition and its implications for regulatory harmonization. A technological overview covers key AI subtypes, including machine learning, artificial neural networks, evolutionary algorithms, generative AI, and inventive AI, along with their different operational levels. The chapter then classifies AI-related outputs, distinguishing between AI-assisted inventions and AI-generated inventions, the latter further subdivided into semi-autonomous, highly autonomous, and fully autonomous generation modes. Finally, it examines key industrial sectors, particularly pharmaceuticals and medical technologies, where AI applications are most promising and AI-generated inventions are increasingly relevant.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Discovering new high-performance materials and alloys is often likened to finding a needle in a haystack because the design space of chemical compositions and processing conditions is astronomically large, and the discovery process is laborious and prohibitively costly. This perspective articulates a research agenda for autonomous materials and metallurgy discovery platforms that combine closed-loop machine learning with robotic experimentation and traditional materials engineering precepts to formulate, process, and test candidate materials with reduced human intervention, and to iterate recursively for stepwise optimization. It explores how sequential learning methods, generative modeling, and hybrid model-based strategies can analyze multimodal experimental data and propose new compositions and processing schedules for subsequent experiments. This approach has the potential to considerably accelerate the pace of discoveries, from decades to mere weeks. Representation learning for material formulations, the injection of domain knowledge into decision-making, and the mechatronic design of robotics that can safely execute harsh processing are all explored as essential components in closing the autonomous loop. Surveyed exemplars show order-of-magnitude improvements in experimental throughput and discovery efficiency. Furthermore, the paper proposes a multidimensional framework for classifying and evaluating the autonomy, complexity, and integration levels of self-driving laboratories, intended to give researchers and practitioners a structured approach to benchmarking future developments in the field. The perspective concludes with an analysis of data infrastructure, simulation coupling, robustness, and human-machine collaboration, distilled into a structured research agenda whose pursuit would broaden adoption across energy, aerospace, and other sectors.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Self-driving laboratories are transforming experimental science, shifting laboratory operation from human-centric schedules towards continuous robotic execution. Beyond accelerating discovery, this transition creates new flexibility in when scientific research consumes electricity, offering an opportunity to coordinate experimental activity with changing electricity-system conditions. Here, we develop and deploy a dynamic, sustainability-aware laboratory-level scheduling framework that combines reinforcement learning with constraint programming to jointly optimize completion time and electricity cost under scientific constraints. Physical execution of 36 experimental tasks spanning six chemical workflow categories shortened completion time by 39.1% and reduced estimated electricity costs by 28.9% relative to a simulated human-centric scheduling baseline. Across five representative tariff cases, estimated per-workflow savings were equivalent to the cost of 0.83–9.14 kWh of off-peak electricity. Our findings demonstrate how self-driving laboratories can translate operational freedom into electricity-demand flexibility, establishing energy responsiveness as a design consideration for scientific research infrastructure.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Process systems engineering (PSE) is broadly about developing methods to guide chemical engineering decisions on the synthesis and analysis of process systems. This definition of Takamatsu (1983) still holds for our field, and so does the problem he left open for us, namely how to synthesise a process system inside a larger system, the world around it, which sets its inputs, outputs and objectives and which it can neither control nor know in advance. Every large process system is unique. It is built once, at one place and time, and it lives only one future. Many such plants, among them the first lignocellulosic biorefineries after 2004, worked technically and then closed. They did not close for lack of optimisation, since our literature had optimised such concepts in great detail. They closed because the world moved in a way the design could not answer. When ruin is possible, the average is the wrong quantity to design for, because a plant that is ruined does not get to live the average. We therefore argue that PSE should study the survival behaviour of process systems, and of the strategies by which we design, build and operate them, under a future that cannot be known in advance. We cannot predict that future, but we can learn to design process systems that survive it. What such a study teaches first is an order of decisions: find what would ruin the plant, then remove that exposure, reserve options that let the plant respond, choose another process, or decide not to build, and only then optimise among the designs that survive. We present the first elements of a methodology for this, illustrate it with two process systems from our own work, e-kerosene and modular pharmaceutical manufacturing, and close with the open questions of this new direction.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Traditional lithium extraction methods are time-consuming and energy-intensive, often leaving a large environmental footprint due to significant freshwater consumption. However, direct lithium extraction (DLE) technologies offer a more efficient and sustainable alternative. DLE can reduce the production time and energy consumption of the overall system, leading to lower costs. This technology is especially promising for extracting lithium from low-concentration brine such as seawater, which contains 8000 times more lithium than land sources. With global demand for lithium expected to reach a third of commercially available land-brine reserves by 2050, DLE’s potential to tap into the vast ocean reserves is crucial. In this review, we assess DLE’s commercial potential, providing an overview of the technology and examining current commercially deployed systems.

Abstract:
Intensity-based two-photon microscopy (2PM) is a cornerstone of biomedical research but lacks the ability to measure concentrations, a pivotal task for longitudinal studies and quantitative comparisons. Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging (FLIM) based on Time-Correlated Single Photon Counting (TCSPC) can overcome those limits but suffers from “pile-up” distortions at high photon count rates, severely limiting acquisition speed. We introduce the “laser period blind time” (LPBT) method to correct pile-up distortions in photon counting electronics, enabling reliable low-cost TCSPC-FLIM at high count rates. The correction was implemented on low-cost hardware based on a field programable gate array (FPGA) and validated using a combination of in silico simulations and in vitro, ex vivo and in vivo measurements. The LBPT approach achieves <3% error in lifetime measurements at count rates more than ten times higher than traditional limits, allowing robust FLIM imaging of sub-second metabolite dynamics with subcellular resolution. Our work enables high-precision, cost-effective FLIM imaging at rates comparable to commercial systems and at a fraction of the cost, facilitating the adoption of FLIM across all areas of research needing affordable, quantitative live imaging solutions.

Abstract:
Nearly a quarter of a century ago, we wrote a review paper about the very new technology of chemical vapour deposition (CVD) of diamond thin films. We now update this review and bring the story up to date by describing the progress made—or not made—over the intervening years. Back in the 1990s and early 2000s, there was enormous excitement about the plethora of applications that were suddenly possible now that diamonds could be fabricated in the form of thin films. Diamond was hailed as the ultimate semiconductor, and it was believed that the few remaining problems would be quickly solved, leading to a new ‘diamond age’ of electronics. In reality, however, difficulty in making large-area diamond wafers and the elusiveness of a useful n-type dopant slowed progress substantially. Unsurprisingly, over the following decade, the enthusiasm and funding for diamonds faded, while competing materials forged ahead. But in the early 2010s, several new game-changing applications for diamonds were discovered, such as electrochemical electrodes, the nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre defect that promised room-temperature quantum computers, and methods to grow large single-crystal gemstone-quality diamonds. These led to a resurgence in diamond research and a new hope that diamond might finally live up to its promise. This article is part of the theme issue ‘Science into the next millennium: 25 years on’.

Abstract:
The management of municipal solid waste remains a critical environmental and energy challenge across the European Union (EU), where a significant portion of waste still ends up in landfills, generating landfill gas (LFG) rich in methane and harmful impurities. In Latvia, despite national strategies to enhance circularity, untreated LFG is underutilized due to inadequate purification infrastructure, particularly in meeting biomethane standards. This study addressed this gap by proposing and evaluating an innovative, multistep LFG purification system tailored to Latvian conditions, with the aim of enabling the broader use of LFG for energy cogeneration and potentially biomethane injection. The research objective was to design, describe, and preliminarily assess a pilot-scale LFG purification prototype suitable for deployment at Latvia’s largest landfill facility—Landfill A. The methodological approach combined chemical composition analysis of LFG, technical site assessments, and engineering modelling of a five-step purification system, including desulfurization, cooling and moisture removal, siloxane filtration, pumping stabilization, and activated carbon treatment. The system was designed for a nominal gas flow rate of 1500 m3/h and developed with modular scalability in mind. The results showed that raw LFG from Landfill A contains high concentrations of hydrogen sulfide, siloxanes, and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), far exceeding permissible thresholds for biomethane applications. The designed prototype demonstrated the technical feasibility of reducing hydrogen sulfide (H2S) concentrations to <7 mg/m3 and siloxanes to ≤0.3 mg/m3, thus aligning the purified gas with EU biomethane quality requirements. Infrastructure assessments confirmed that existing electricity, water, and sewage capacities at Landfill A are sufficient to support the system’s operation. The implications of this research suggest that properly engineered LFG purification systems can transform landfills from passive waste sinks into active energy resources, aligning with the EU Green Deal goals and enhancing local energy resilience. It is recommended that further validation be carried out through long-term pilot operation, economic analysis of gas recovery profitability, and adaptation of the system for integration with national gas grids. The prototype provides a transferable model for other Baltic and Eastern European contexts, where LFG remains an underexploited asset for sustainable energy transitions.

Abstract:
Abstract Time‐restricted feeding (TRF) holds promise for alleviating cognitive decline in aging, albeit the precise mechanism via the gut‐brain axis remains elusive. In a clinical trial, we observed, for the first time, that a 4‐month TRF ameliorated cognitive impairments among Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients. Experiments in 5xFAD mice corroborated the gut microbiota‐dependent effect of TRF on mitigating cognitive dysfunction, amyloid‐beta deposition, and neuroinflammation. Multi‐omics integration linked Bifidobacterium pseudolongum (B. pseudolongum) and propionic acid (PA) with key genes in AD pathogenesis. Oral supplementation of B. pseudolongum or PA mimicked TRF's protective effects. Positron emission tomography imaging confirmed PA's blood‐brain barrier penetration, while knockdown of the free fatty acid receptor 3 (FFAR3) diminished TRF's cognitive benefits. Notably, we observed a positive correlation between fecal PA and improved cognitive function in an AD cohort, further indicating that TRF enhanced PA production. These findings highlight the microbiota‐metabolites‐brain axis as pivotal in TRF's cognitive benefits, proposing B. pseudolongum or PA as potential AD therapies.

Single nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond have been used extensively for high-sensitivity nanoscale sensing, but conventional approaches use confocal microscopy to measure individual centers sequentially, limiting throughput and access to non-local physical properties. Here we design and implement a multiplexed NV sensing platform that allows us to read out many single NV centers simultaneously using a low-noise camera. Using this platform, we coherently manipulate and read out the spin states of hundreds of individual NV centers in parallel, achieving comparable magnetic field sensitivity to confocal measurements. We also implement a parallelized version of spin-to-charge-conversion readout for low NV center spin state readout noise and use it to demonstrate multiplexed covariance magnetometry, in which we measure six two-point magnetic field correlators from four NV centers simultaneously. The number of correlators we can measure is limited only by the available laser power, opening the door to massively multiplexed covariance magnetometry. Our platform significantly increases the throughput and broadens the applications of nanoscale sensing using diamond quantum sensors.

 Cloud labs are remote facilities packed with equipment to which researchers can outsource their experimental work.
 Working 24/7 and 365 days a year, such labs offer scientists anywhere the opportunity to gather data without needing
